chapter: Joe Oliver, Tom Brown and closing
title: Joe Oliver compared with Louis Armstrong
summary: He describes Oliver's dirty tone and mute use, how Louis learned from him, and anecdotes about Oliver's eye and derby.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Remembering King Oliver: the man, the band, the decline

blocks.x: You mentioned once before that the three great musicians, Snoozer of course we were talking about, and Louie and Bix, you didn't mention Joe Oliver. At other times you've told me you thought Joe Oliver had something that Louie never quite got. We all know Louie, he's wonderful. I'm trying to knock in.

Yeah, I think, well of course Louie doesn't have much resemblance to Joe Oliver anymore, although I think he's, uh, contrary to most, uh, died in the world jazz people, I think he's a very great performer, jazz performer today. He just hasn't been in good settings. But Joe Oliver had a dirty tone, which Louie almost got to perfection when Louie first hit New York. Of course Louie, uh, breathed on, on everything that Joe Oliver did, you know? Yeah. I mean, he studied Joe Oliver as close as a person could ever study anybody. Uh, Joe Oliver had, had that dirty tone, which, uh, which jazz people have come to love so much. Uh, and, uh, I can't say that, that, that, uh, that Louie missed it much. Uh, like, uh, like the records of Everybody Loves My Baby and, uh, and, yeah, those Clarence Williams records. I don't think Louie was very far away from that dirty tone at that time. Since then, of course, he's gotten a good way away from it, yeah. But it takes too much of a person's lip to play like that. It's a, oh, it's a unbelievable, uh, uh, uh, strain on your lip. You see, Joe Oliver played with a mute in his hand. Uh, the mute was halfway in his bell. And right there is a strain on your lip. You're not holding the cornet, uh, with, with the ease that you should hold it, you see? And, uh, uh, the way he worked his hand in and out of there, uh, to help bend those notes, and the dirty sound he got, well, the, the nearest thing I've ever heard was Louie to that. Uh, as I, as I told you before, Joe used to really knock me out of my mind up at Tulane Gym. Yeah. Oh, one cute thing I'd like to tell you about, uh, Joe Oliver. Uh, he was a very supercilious Negro, you know? He knew what he had. He was, uh, he was a big boy in, in, in music in New Orleans. Yeah. He had all the jobs tied up, you see? And he took nothing from nobody. So sometimes, uh, he'd play, uh, after a tune was over, somebody would come up and ask him, uh, what was that tune you played last? And he, he'd say, uh, who struck John? No matter what it was, you know? Yeah. If it was a nice little girl who would ask him, or a boy or somebody, he cared nothing for none of them, you know? Yeah. Another funny thing he used to do, he had a, he had skin over his eyes, I don't know what you, over one eye. And his eye was, uh, I don't know whether they call it cataract or not, but the skin was growing over his eye, one eye. And that eye was cocked, too. It was looking out towards the left, you see? Yeah. Well, he, he always had a brown derby. And he put his brown derby when he was playing over there, he used it for, uh, for a mute, too, sometimes, you know? He used, uh, he, uh, put that over his good eye and he'd stare out into space over to the left with that cock eye, you know? He was a real sassy nigga, I'm telling you. Cute as hell. Mean, too, boy. He was, he was really mean, yeah. He was, uh, yes, sir. It sure was fun to watch that guy. I mean, he had that band under control, too, boy. He was the boss. He was the boss. Yes, sir.
